content: 1. Group work should consist of 4 to 6 participants to ensure effective dialogue and active participation from everyone involved. 2. To adapt to participants’ cultural and social contexts, encourage them to provide case examples relevant to the environments in which they will be offering assistance. 3. Invite participants to discuss how Psychological First Aid (PFA) can be tailored to align with their cultural practices and norms. 4. It is expected that both facilitators and participants may make mistakes while demonstrating PFA. This is a normal part of the learning process. 5. To ensure participants understand effective PFA skills and recognize what should be avoided, summarize the key points or “take-home messages” at the conclusion of all practice activities. 6. Write the main points on a flip chart or display them on slides, and refer to the two-page PFA pocket guide for clarity. 7. Effective time management is critical for successful facilitation. The provided agenda serves as a guideline for timing the orientation. 8. Be prepared for variations in the duration of role plays or exercises, and allocate additional time for clarification of complex topics if necessary. 9. To manage time effectively, schedule arrival and registration before the training begins, start and end sessions on time, and adhere to the general schedule, including short breaks. 10. Avoid spending excessive time on slides; instead, prioritize discussions, role plays, and simulations, as these activities are where most learning occurs. 11. Ensure role plays are time-bound to prevent them from becoming overly lengthy. 12. If a translator is used, anticipate that the orientation may take longer than planned. 13. During the orientation, participants should understand the overall aims, agenda, and methods, and agree on ground rules to foster a productive and supportive working environment. 14. The orientation will focus on practical skills and interactive activities, allowing participants to practice and learn from one another. 15. Participation is essential, and everyone will have the opportunity to practice in front of their peers. Mistakes are part of the learning process and should be embraced as opportunities for growth. 16. Ground rules should include punctuality, turning off cell phones, respecting confidentiality, avoiding interruptions, and providing constructive feedback. 17. Participants should be sensitive to one another, as the orientation may touch on distressing stories or personal experiences. Facilitators should offer support to anyone who feels uncomfortable. 18. A pre-test may be administered to assess participants’ baseline knowledge and confidence in providing PFA and staying safe during an Ebola outbreak. This test can be repeated post-orientation to measure the impact of the training. 19. Participants should gain a clear understanding of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD), including its transmission, prevention, and how this knowledge applies to providing PFA. 20. Accurate information about EVD is essential to support others effectively, prevent infection, and reduce fear, panic, and stigma. 21. EVD is a severe infectious disease that can be fatal. However, survival chances increase significantly with adequate healthcare, and the spread of the disease can be reduced through proper infection prevention and control measures. 22. Individuals are at risk of EVD if they have been in contact with someone sick with Ebola or attended the funeral of someone who died with Ebola symptoms, as they may have touched the infected person. 23. The symptoms of Ebola begin suddenly with a high fever, fatigue, headache, and body aches, followed by vomiting, diarrhea, and, in severe cases, bleeding. Non-fatal cases may show improvement around days 6 to 11. 24. Early treatment increases survival chances and prevents the spread of the disease. If someone is suspected of having Ebola, they should seek medical attention immediately at an Ebola Treatment Centre. 25. Caregivers and healthcare workers must use personal protective equipment (PPE) to prevent infection. PPE includes heavy clothing, gloves, goggles, and masks. 26. While waiting for specialized support, families should protect themselves by isolating the sick person, avoiding direct contact, and ensuring proper hygiene practices, such as frequent handwashing with soap and water or alcohol-based sanitizer. 27. Provide the sick person with their own separate space and personal items, and ensure only one person cares for them to minimize exposure. 28. Offer plenty of fluids, such as water, soup, or tea, and administer paracetamol for fever or pain. Avoid giving aspirin or other painkillers. 29. Be vigilant for danger signs such as vomiting, diarrhea, or bleeding, as these symptoms indicate a high risk of infecting others or death. In such cases, the patient should be transported to a hospital or treatment center immediately by trained health workers using PPE. 30. Community members who have fully recovered from Ebola can assist in caring for sick individuals, as they have developed immunity to the virus. 31. Participants should be informed about available local resources and services to cope with an Ebola outbreak, including contact details for community leaders and Ebola hotlines. 32. Emphasize the importance of handwashing after any contact with a sick person, their belongings, or potentially contaminated items, even if gloves were worn. 33. Encourage participants to share additional contact details and resources they are aware of with the group to enhance collective preparedness and response.
